title: Maximum AND Sum of Array
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` of length `n` and an integer `numSlots`, where `2 * numSlots >= n`. The slots are labelled `1` through `numSlots`, and every number of `nums` must go into some slot, with no slot holding more than two numbers (a slot may stay empty).

A placement scores the sum, over all numbers, of `number AND label`, where `AND` is bitwise and and `label` is the slot the number went into. Return the highest score any placement can reach.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every slot for every number costs up to `numSlots^n`, about 9^18. The slots are few, though: give each slot two **positions**, so there are `2 * numSlots <= 18` positions and a set of filled positions fits in an 18-bit `mask`. If numbers are always placed in order, the number of set bits in `mask` tells how many have been placed, so `dp[mask]` (the best score for filling exactly those positions with the first numbers) is a complete state.

## Approach

1. Positions `j = 0 .. 2 * numSlots - 1` belong to slot `(j >> 1) + 1`; `full = 1 << positions` masks exist.
2. Walk masks in increasing order. `ones[mask]` (built from `ones[mask >> 1]`) counts its set bits, and `i = ones[mask] - 1` is the index of the last number placed. Skip masks with more bits than `n`.
3. Number `i` sits in one of the set positions `j`. Removing that bit gives a smaller mask, already final, so `dp[mask]` is the best `dp[mask ^ (1 << j)] + (nums[i] & slot)`.
4. When `i === n - 1` every number is placed; keep the largest such `dp[mask]` in `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1,2,3,4,5,6]`, `numSlots = 3`, so 6 positions and 64 masks. `dp[0b000001] = 1 & 1 = 1` (number 1 in slot 1). `dp[0b000101] = 3`: 1 in slot 1 and 2 in slot 2 (positions 0 and 2). Continuing, the mask `0b111111` with all six bits gets `dp = 9`, reached by 1 and 4 in slot 1, 2 and 6 in slot 2, 3 and 5 in slot 3: `1+0+2+2+3+1 = 9`. No other placement does better, so `best = 9`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(4^numSlots · numSlots): `2^(2·numSlots)` masks, each trying `2·numSlots` bits (about 4.7 million steps at most).
- Space: O(4^numSlots) for `dp` and `ones`.

## Pitfalls

- A slot holds two numbers, so give it two bits; a single bit per slot would forbid sharing.
- The answer is not `dp[full - 1]` unless `n = 2 * numSlots`; take the best over masks with exactly `n` bits.
- Slot labels start at 1: position `j` is slot `(j >> 1) + 1`, not `j >> 1`.
- Parenthesise `nums[i] & slot`; `+` binds tighter than `&` in JavaScript.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | how many numbers must be placed |
| `positions` | two positions per slot, `2 * numSlots` |
| `full` | number of masks, `1 << positions` |
| `ones` | set-bit count of each mask |
| `dp` | best score for filling the positions of `mask` with the first numbers |
| `mask`, `j`, `slot` | current set of positions, the position of the last number, its slot label |
| `i` | index of the number placed last in `mask` |
| `best` | best score with all `n` numbers placed |

narration.3: Each slot gets two positions, one for each number it can hold.
narration.4: Every subset of positions is a mask below this bound.
narration.5: ones[mask] will hold how many bits mask has set.
narration.6: dp[mask] is the best score for filling exactly these positions with the first numbers.

narration.10: Count the bits of mask from the count of mask without its lowest bit.

narration.15: Try each position as the place of number i.
narration.16: Only positions that are filled in this mask qualify.
narration.17: Two neighbouring positions share a slot, labelled from 1.
narration.18: Score of the rest of the mask plus number i AND its slot label.
narration.21: All n numbers are placed in this mask...
narration.22: ...so it is a complete placement; keep the best.
narration.25: The highest score over every complete placement.
